```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA, message = TRUE, warning = TRUE)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(tibble)

# Formatting helpers for numbers and p-values
fmt_num <- function(x, digits = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "NA", ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
```

```{r ensure-run, echo=FALSE}
if (!file.exists("results/tables/anova_or_kruskal_tn.csv")) {
  message("Analysis outputs not found — sourcing analysis script...")
  source("analysis_landuse_nutrients.R")
}
```

## Executive Summary

This course-level analysis of a NAWQA nutrient subset shows clear land-use effects on stream nutrients. Key results:

- TN and TP differ strongly among Agricultural, Urban, and Forest catchments.
- Agricultural and urban sites have higher TN/TP; forested sites are lowest.
- TN increases with agricultural land cover (R²≈0.41) based on simple linear regression.
- High TN (and TP) occur more frequently in agricultural and urban sites than in forested sites.

## Introduction

Land-use change can affect downstream river water quality through nutrient inputs and retention processes. Agricultural and urban catchments typically export more nitrogen (TN) and phosphorus (TP) due to fertiliser application and runoff, whereas forested catchments often retain nutrients more effectively. This study uses a small, reproducible subset of NAWQA nutrient data to test whether TN and TP differ among land-use types (Agricultural, Urban, Forest) and to examine how land-use percentages (pAG, pURB) relate to TN and TP.

## Data and Methods

- Dataset: `data/nawqa_landuse_nutrients_subset.csv` with 120 river stations (≈40 per land-use type). Variables include LandUseType, TN, TP, pAG (% agricultural), pURB (% urban), pFOR (% forest), and coordinates.
- Pre-processing: constructed `log10TN` and `log10TP` to improve normality and variance homogeneity; performed Shapiro–Wilk normality tests and Levene’s tests (see `results/tables/assumption_checks.csv`).
- Analysis plan (course-level tests only):
  - TN ~ LandUseType: Kruskal–Wallis (nonparametric) with Dunn-type post hoc, because normality and/or equal variances were violated (especially Urban group).
  - TP ~ LandUseType: Kruskal–Wallis with post hoc comparisons; log10 improved assumptions but Urban still deviated from normality.
  - TN (Agricultural vs Forest): after log10 transform, assumptions acceptable; used independent-samples Student t-test on `log10TN`.
  - pAG vs TN: Pearson and Spearman correlations; simple linear regression TN ~ pAG.
  - pURB vs TP: Pearson and Spearman correlations; simple linear regression TP ~ pURB, emphasising Spearman when Pearson was weak.
  - HighTN/HighTP vs LandUseType: defined HighTN/HighTP as ≥ 75th percentile; used chi-square tests of independence.

```{r method_map, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tibble); library(knitr)
method_map <- tribble(
  ~Question, ~Test_Used, ~Assumptions, ~Evidence_File,
  "TN ~ LandUseType (3 groups)", "Kruskal–Wallis + Dunn", "Non-normal / heteroscedastic", "results/tables/anova_or_kruskal_tn.csv",
  "TP ~ LandUseType (3 groups)", "Kruskal–Wallis + Dunn", "Non-normal even after log10", "results/tables/anova_or_kruskal_tp.csv",
  "TN: Ag vs Forest (2 groups)", "Student t-test on log10TN", "Approx. normal & equal variances after log10", "results/tables/tn_ag_vs_for_test.csv",
  "pAG vs TN", "Pearson + OLS; Spearman robustness", "Continuous; linear/monotonic", "results/tables/correlation_regression_pAG_TN.csv",
  "pURB vs TP", "Spearman primary; Pearson/OLS descriptive", "Linear weak; monotonic significant", "results/tables/correlation_regression_pURB_TP.csv",
  "HighTN × LandUseType", "Chi-square", "Counts by group", "results/tables/chisq_highTN.csv"
)
kable(method_map, align = "l", caption = "Methods mapping: question → test → assumptions → evidence file")
```

## Results

```{r results-setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

# If results do not exist yet, run the analysis script
if (!file.exists("results/tables/anova_or_kruskal_tn.csv")) {
  source("analysis_landuse_nutrients.R")
}

# Load key tables
assump_t      <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/assumption_checks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anova_tn      <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/anova_or_kruskal_tn.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anova_tp      <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/anova_or_kruskal_tp.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
posthoc_tn    <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/posthoc_tn.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
posthoc_tp    <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/posthoc_tp.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
ttest_af      <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/tn_ag_vs_for_test.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
corr_pAG_TN   <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/correlation_regression_pAG_TN.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
corr_pURB_TP  <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/correlation_regression_pURB_TP.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
chisq_highTN  <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/chisq_highTN.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
chisq_highTP  <- readr::read_csv("results/tables/chisq_highTP.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

### 3.1 Assumption checks

Shapiro–Wilk tests indicate strong non-normality for TN and TP on the raw scale; `log10TN`/`log10TP` improve normality and Levene’s tests show acceptable variance homogeneity on the log scale, though Urban sometimes still deviates slightly. Below is a compact subset of the assumption table.

```{r show-assumptions, echo=FALSE}
assump_view <- assump_t %>%
  filter((test == "Shapiro-Wilk" & variable %in% c("TN","TP") & scale %in% c("raw","log10")) |
           (test == "Levene" & variable %in% c("TN","TP"))) %>%
  head(20)
knitr::kable(assump_view, caption = "Assumption checks: Shapiro–Wilk (by group) and Levene (across groups)")
```

### 3.2 Differences in TN among land-use types (Kruskal–Wallis)

The Kruskal–Wallis test shows TN differs among Agricultural, Urban, and Forest sites; post hoc comparisons indicate Agricultural > Urban > Forest.

```{r A-tables, echo=FALSE}
# Format p-values to avoid rendering as 0e+00 for extremely small numbers
anova_tn_fmt <- anova_tn %>% mutate(p_value = fmt_p(p_value))
posthoc_tn_fmt <- posthoc_tn %>% mutate(
  p_adj = ifelse(is.na(p_adj), NA_character_,
                 ifelse(p_adj < 1e-12, "<1e-12", formatC(p_adj, format = "e", digits = 2)))
)
knitr::kable(anova_tn_fmt, caption = "Main test for TN across LandUseType (Kruskal–Wallis)")
knitr::kable(posthoc_tn_fmt, caption = "Post hoc pairwise comparisons for TN (BH-adjusted)")
```

```{r A-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width='75%', fig.cap='Figure 1. Distribution of TN concentrations by land-use type.'}
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/fig1_tn_boxplot.png")
```

### 3.3 Differences in TP among land-use types (Kruskal–Wallis)

The Kruskal–Wallis test shows TP differs among land-use types. Forest has much lower TP than Agricultural and Urban, while Agricultural vs Urban is not significant.

```{r B-tables, echo=FALSE}
anova_tp_fmt <- anova_tp %>% mutate(p_value = fmt_p(p_value))
posthoc_tp_fmt <- posthoc_tp %>% mutate(
  p_adj = ifelse(is.na(p_adj), NA_character_,
                 ifelse(p_adj < 1e-12, "<1e-12", formatC(p_adj, format = "e", digits = 2)))
)
knitr::kable(anova_tp_fmt, caption = "Main test for TP across LandUseType (Kruskal–Wallis)")
knitr::kable(posthoc_tp_fmt, caption = "Post hoc pairwise comparisons for TP (BH-adjusted)")
```

```{r B-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width='75%', fig.cap='Figure 2. Distribution of TP concentrations by land-use type.'}
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/fig2_tp_boxplot.png")
```

### 3.4 TN: Agricultural vs Forest (t-test on log10TN)

After log10 transform, assumptions were acceptable; we used an independent-samples Student t-test on `log10TN`.

```{r C-tables, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(ttest_af, caption = "Two-sample test for TN: Agricultural vs Forest (on log10TN)")
```

```{r C-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width='75%', fig.cap='Figure 3. TN for Agricultural vs Forest.'}
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/fig3_tn_two_groups.png")
```

```{r C-ci, echo=FALSE}
# Recompute t-test and 95% CI on log10 scale; also back-transform to ratio of geometric means
dat_full <- readr::read_csv("data/nawqa_landuse_nutrients_subset.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dat_af   <- dat_full %>% filter(LandUseType %in% c("Agricultural","Forest")) %>% droplevels()
tt <- t.test(log10(TN) ~ LandUseType, data = dat_af, var.equal = TRUE)

# Group means (original scale)
grp_stats <- dat_af %>% group_by(LandUseType) %>% summarise(mean_TN = mean(TN, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = LandUseType, values_from = mean_TN)

ci_log10 <- as.numeric(tt$conf.int)
ratio_geo <- 10^ci_log10  # ratio of geometric means (Agricultural vs Forest)

ci_table <- tibble(
  metric = c("t statistic", "df", "p-value",
             "Mean TN (Ag, mg/L)", "Mean TN (Forest, mg/L)",
             "95% CI for mean diff (log10TN)",
             "95% CI for ratio of geometric means (Ag/Forest)"),
  value  = c(fmt_num(unname(tt$statistic), 2), fmt_num(unname(tt$parameter), 0), fmt_p(tt$p.value),
             fmt_num(grp_stats$Agricultural, 2), fmt_num(grp_stats$Forest, 2),
             paste0("[", fmt_num(ci_log10[1], 3), ", ", fmt_num(ci_log10[2], 3), "]"),
             paste0("[", fmt_num(ratio_geo[1], 2), "x, ", fmt_num(ratio_geo[2], 2), "x]"))
)
knitr::kable(ci_table, col.names = c("Statistic", "Value"), caption = "t-test details with 95% confidence intervals (log10 scale and back-transformed ratios)")
```

### 3.5 Relationship between agricultural land and TN (correlation & regression)

Pearson and Spearman correlations indicate strong positive association between pAG and TN; the simple linear regression explains about 40% of variance.

```{r D1-table, echo=FALSE}
# Format correlation/regression summary to avoid p-values shown as 0
corr_pAG_TN_fmt <- corr_pAG_TN %>%
  mutate(
    Pearson_r = fmt_num(Pearson_r, 3),
    Pearson_p = fmt_p(Pearson_p),
    Spearman_rho = fmt_num(Spearman_rho, 3),
    Spearman_p = fmt_p(Spearman_p),
    Slope = fmt_num(Slope, 3),
    Intercept = fmt_num(Intercept, 3),
    R2 = fmt_num(R2, 3),
    F_stat = fmt_num(F_stat, 2),
    df1 = as.integer(df1),
    df2 = as.integer(df2),
    F_p = fmt_p(F_p)
  )
knitr::kable(corr_pAG_TN_fmt, caption = "Correlation and regression summary: pAG vs TN")
```

```{r D1-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width='75%', fig.cap='Figure 4. TN vs agricultural land (%) with least-squares line and 95% CI.'}
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/fig4_pAG_TN_scatter.png")
```

```{r D1-ci, echo=FALSE}
# Refit OLS and extract slope CI for completeness
dat_full <- readr::read_csv("data/nawqa_landuse_nutrients_subset.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_pag <- lm(TN ~ pAG, data = dat_full)
ci_pag  <- confint(fit_pag)["pAG", ]
summ_pag <- tibble(
  Slope = fmt_num(coef(fit_pag)["pAG"], 4),
  Intercept = fmt_num(coef(fit_pag)["(Intercept)"], 3),
  R2 = fmt_num(summary(fit_pag)$r.squared, 3),
  CI_95 = paste0("[", fmt_num(ci_pag[1], 4), ", ", fmt_num(ci_pag[2], 4), "]")
)
knitr::kable(summ_pag, caption = "OLS slope and 95% CI: TN ~ pAG")
```

### 3.6 Relationship between urban land and TP (correlation & regression)

Pearson correlation is weak/non-significant, whereas Spearman is significantly positive; the linear regression has low R².

```{r D2-table, echo=FALSE}

  mutate(
    Pearson_r = fmt_num(Pearson_r, 3),
    Pearson_p = fmt_p(Pearson_p),
    Spearman_rho = fmt_num(Spearman_rho, 3),
    Spearman_p = fmt_p(Spearman_p),
    Slope = fmt_num(Slope, 5),
    Intercept = fmt_num(Intercept, 3),
    R2 = fmt_num(R2, 3),
    F_stat = fmt_num(F_stat, 2),
    df1 = as.integer(df1),
    df2 = as.integer(df2),
    F_p = fmt_p(F_p)
  )
knitr::kable(corr_pURB_TP_fmt, caption = "Correlation and regression summary: pURB vs TP")
```

```{r D2-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width='75%', fig.cap='Figure 5. TP vs urban land (%) with least-squares line and 95% CI.'}
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/fig5_pURB_TP_scatter.png")
```

```{r D2-ci, echo=FALSE}
dat_full <- readr::read_csv("data/nawqa_landuse_nutrients_subset.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fit_purb <- lm(TP ~ pURB, data = dat_full)
ci_purb  <- confint(fit_purb)["pURB", ]
summ_purb <- tibble(
  Slope = fmt_num(coef(fit_purb)["pURB"], 5),
  Intercept = fmt_num(coef(fit_purb)["(Intercept)"], 3),
  R2 = fmt_num(summary(fit_purb)$r.squared, 3),
  CI_95 = paste0("[", fmt_num(ci_purb[1], 5), ", ", fmt_num(ci_purb[2], 5), "]")
)
knitr::kable(summ_purb, caption = "OLS slope and 95% CI: TP ~ pURB")
```

### 3.7 Association between land-use type and high TN/TP (Chi-square)

Chi-square tests indicate that the proportion of high-TN (and high-TP) sites differs by land-use type.

```{r E-tables, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(chisq_highTN, caption = "Chi-square test: HighTN and LandUseType")
knitr::kable(chisq_highTP, caption = "Chi-square test: HighTP and LandUseType")
```

```{r E-figure, echo=FALSE, out.width='75%', fig.cap='Figure 6. Proportion of stations with High TN by land-use type.'}

```

### 3.X Results at a Glance

```{r glance, echo=FALSE}
# Build a one-page summary using numbers from the loaded tables
tn_stat <- anova_tn$statistic[1]; tp_stat <- anova_tp$statistic[1]
tn_p <- anova_tn$p_value[1]; tp_p <- anova_tp$p_value[1]
glance <- tribble(
  ~Finding, ~Evidence,
  "TN: Agricultural > Urban > Forest", paste0("Kruskal–Wallis \u03C7\u00B2\u2248", fmt_num(tn_stat,1), ", p=", fmt_p(tn_p), "; Dunn post hoc all pairs p<1e-7"),
  "TP: Forest << Agricultural \u2248 Urban", paste0("Kruskal–Wallis \u03C7\u00B2\u2248", fmt_num(tp_stat,1), ", p=", fmt_p(tp_p), "; Ag–Ur ns"),
  "TN (Ag vs Forest, 2 groups)", "t(log10TN)=13.9, df=78, p<1e-22; 95% CI suggests large difference",
  "pAG \u2191 TN", "Pearson r\u22480.64, R\u00B2\u22480.41, p<1e-14; slope CI > 0",
  "pURB \u2191 TP (monotonic)", "Spearman \u03C1\u22480.45, p<1e-6; linear slope small, R\u00B2\u22480.02",
  "HighTN by land-use type", "Chi-square \u03C7\u00B2\u224846.7, p<1e-10; highest in Ag/Urban"
)
knitr::kable(glance, align = "l", caption = "Results at a glance: key findings and evidence")
```

## Discussion

Our course-level analyses consistently show that land-use influences nutrient concentrations. First, Kruskal–Wallis tests indicate strong differences in TN and TP among land-use types: agricultural and urban catchments exhibit higher nutrient levels, whereas forested catchments are lower. Post hoc comparisons confirm Forest < Agricultural and Forest < Urban for both TN and TP; Agricultural vs Urban is clear for TN but not significant for TP.

Second, relationships with land-use percentages align with expectations. TN increases with agricultural land cover: correlations are strong (Pearson and Spearman) and the simple linear regression explains ≈40% of variance. TP vs urban land cover shows a weaker linear association (low R², non-significant Pearson) but a significant monotonic trend (Spearman), consistent with heterogeneous urban runoff patterns.

Third, chi-square tests show that high-nutrient stations (≥ 75th percentile) are more frequent in agricultural and urban catchments than in forested catchments, reinforcing the group comparison results.

Methodologically, we used Kruskal–Wallis in place of ANOVA where assumption checks (Shapiro–Wilk and Levene) indicated violations, and we used a log10 t-test for two-group TN comparisons where assumptions were acceptable post-transform. The 95% CI for the mean difference in log10TN indicates agricultural sites have several-fold higher TN than forests (ratio of geometric means CI excludes 1). For pURB–TP, the slope CI is small and close to zero, consistent with the weak linear relationship despite a significant monotonic trend. These choices follow standard introductory flow charts. Limitations include cross-sectional design, potential confounding (e.g., hydrology, point sources), and coarse land-use classes.

## Conclusion (optional)

In this subset of NAWQA nutrient data, land-use type is a strong determinant of TN and TP. Agricultural > Urban > Forest for TN, and Forest is clearly lowest for TP. TN scales positively with agricultural land cover; TP shows a weaker linear but significant monotonic association with urban land cover. These results provide a clear, course-level demonstration of land-use impacts on river nutrients.
